parts.title: AgentClinic: a test of how well AI doctors can work with patients, test results and tools
parts.abstract:
Abstract

To know whether a large language model (LLM) could ever help doctors, we need to test it in realistic medical situations. An LLM is a computer program that can read and write human language. Most existing tests ask the model to answer a single question with all the information already given. That does not capture how doctors actually work: they make a series of decisions, one after another, as they learn more.

We built AgentClinic, a test that imitates a real clinic. In it, an AI doctor talks with an AI patient, gathers information from tests and images, and works with different tools, all while starting with incomplete information. This lets us test the models in depth across nine medical specialties and seven languages.

We found that the same medical questions from MedQA, a standard question bank, become much harder when the model has to work them out step by step in AgentClinic. As a result, the share of correct diagnoses can fall to less than one tenth of what it was in the original test. Overall, models built on Claude-3.5 did better than the other models in most settings.

The models differed sharply, though, in how well they used tools. These included learning from past cases, searching for information when they needed it, and reflecting on their own reasoning. Strikingly, Llama-3 improved by up to 92% compared with its performance without the tool when it had a notebook. This notebook lets the doctor write and edit notes that carry over from one patient to the next.

To look more closely at our clinic simulations, we also used real electronic health records, which are patients' medical files stored in a computer. We asked doctors to read and rate the simulations, we gave the models instructions that push them toward known biases, and we explored new ways of measuring the experience from the patient's point of view, which this interactive setting makes possible.

Subject areas: Diagnosis, Medical ethics, Computer science
parts.introduction_first:
One of the main goals of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is to build systems that can interact with people and solve many different kinds of problems. Medical AI shares this goal, hoping to create systems that can solve problems in ways that help patients.

In recent years, many general-purpose large language models (LLMs) have shown that they can solve hard problems, some of which people think are difficult even for humans. One example is the United States Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE), the exam doctors must pass to work in the United States. LLMs quickly overtook the average human score on it. In September 2021 they scored 38.1%, and by November 2023 they scored 90.2%. For comparison, a human needs 60% to pass, and human experts score 87%.

These LLMs are not designed to replace doctors. Even so, they could help make healthcare easier to reach and able to serve more people. More than 40% of the world's population has limited access to healthcare, and the world's healthcare system is under growing strain.
parts.introduction_rest:
Still, these systems have limits that stop them from being used in real clinics. Recently, LLMs have shown that they can store medical knowledge, find the right medical texts, and answer medical questions accurately in a single turn, where the model gives one answer and the conversation ends.

Real medical work is much more complicated. Doctors make a series of decisions, one after another. They have to cope with uncertainty, work with limited information and limited resources, and at the same time care kindly for patients and learn what those patients know. Today's tests do not capture this. Most recent studies use fixed multiple-choice tests, where a short case description gives the model all the information it needs, and the model either answers a question or simply picks the most likely answer.

In this work, we introduce AgentClinic, a test that imitates a real clinic. It is open-source, which means anyone can use and change it. It is also multimodal, meaning it handles different kinds of information, such as words, measurements and medical images. AgentClinic is a benchmark, a standard way to compare how well different models perform.

We improve on earlier work by using AI agents to imitate many parts of a clinic, not just the patient and the doctor. An agent is a computer program that acts like a person. Through conversation with a measurement agent, the AI doctor can carry out simulated medical checks, such as measuring temperature and blood pressure or recording an EKG, which is a recording of the heart's electrical activity. The doctor can also ask the agent to read medical images, such as MRI scans and X-rays.

We also let the agents show 23 different biases, which are known to exist in real clinics. A bias is a habit of thinking that can lead someone to make mistakes. We present clinic settings from 9 medical specialties and in 7 different languages. We also study how well agents work when they are given different tools and different ways of reasoning.

Our ways of measuring performance go beyond how often the doctor gets the diagnosis right. They also focus on the patient, with measures such as patient compliance, meaning how well the patient follows the doctor's advice, and consultation ratings, meaning how well the patient rates the visit.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:
parts.methods:
## Methods

### Who the AI characters are

The AI patient knows a set of symptoms and a medical history that we give it, but it does not know what disease it actually has. Its job is to talk with the AI doctor, describe its symptoms and answer the doctor's questions, so that the conversation feels like a real patient visit.

The AI measurement agent gives the patient realistic medical readings that fit the patient's condition. It lets the doctor ask for particular tests to be done on the patient. We trained this agent on a wide range of test results from our scenario template, the set of medical cases we use, so that it gives the results a patient with that condition would be expected to have. For example, a patient with a heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) might give these results when asked: "Electrocardiogram: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Cardiac Markers: Troponin I: Elevated, Creatine Kinase MB: Elevated. Chest X-Ray: No pulmonary congestion, normal heart size." A patient with Hodgkin's lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, might instead have a long list of blood measurements that are out of the normal range, such as hemoglobin, platelets and white blood cells (WBC).

The AI doctor is the main character we are testing. At the start, it gets only a little background about the patient and a short goal, such as "Evaluate the patient presenting with chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath." We then ask it to work out the patient's symptoms through conversation and by collecting information, until it reaches a diagnosis. The doctor can also ask the measurement agent for test results, naming which test to do, such as a chest X-ray, an EKG (a recording of the heart's electrical activity) or blood pressure. Each time the doctor asks for test results, we count it as one of the questions it has left.

To copy the limits doctors face in real life, the doctor can only ask a limited number of questions of the patient. In our tests, the doctor has a limited number of turns, which we set to 20 for most experiments. One turn is one reply from the doctor followed by one reply from a tool, or from the measurement agent or the patient, depending on what the doctor said. At the end of the last turn, the doctor must give its diagnosis, and a moderator then checks it.

The moderator's job is to decide whether the doctor diagnosed the patient correctly at the end of the session. To do this, it is given the correct answer, which we call the ground truth. We need a moderator because the diagnosis the doctor writes can be very loosely worded, depending on the model, and it has to be read carefully to see whether the doctor reached the right conclusion. For example, the correct diagnosis might be "Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus," but the doctor might say in a loose way: "Given all the information we've gathered, including your symptoms, elevated blood sugar levels, presence of glucose and ketones in your urine, and unintentional weight loss I believe a diagnosis of Type 2 Diabetes with possible insulin resistance is appropriate." The moderator has to decide whether this diagnosis was correct.

The moderator's instructions are: "Here is the correct diagnosis: [correct diagnosis]. Here was the doctor dialogue: [doctor agent's diagnosis]. Are these the same? You are responsible for determine if the correct diagnosis and the doctor diagnosis are the same disease. Please respond only with Yes or No. Nothing else". Sometimes the check gets harder. For example, the doctor might say: "Given your CT and blood results, I believe a diagnosis of PE is the most reasonable conclusion." Here PE (pulmonary embolism, a blood clot in the lungs) is the correct diagnosis, but it is only shortened.

### Measuring how the patient feels

After each conversation between the patient and the doctor, the patient agent gave three ratings on a scale from 1 to 10. This kind of scale is called a Likert-type scale. The three ratings were: (i) how confident the patient felt in the doctor's assessment, (ii) compliance, meaning how likely the patient said they were to follow the recommended treatment, and (iii) consultation willingness, meaning how likely they were to see the same doctor again.

We did not give the model any words to describe each number on the scale (for example, we did not say what a 6 means or how it differs from a 7). So each rating came from the model's own sense of how the conversation was going. We did not run any extra checks to see whether the ratings stayed consistent from one run to the next. Our analyses focus on how the ratings differ between the conditions we compare, such as biased versus unbiased, rather than on what the exact rating numbers mean.

### How accurately doctors diagnose when they have images and test results

To test the models' reasoning more strictly, we wanted them to work out the diagnosis on their own, without being told what to look for. So we did not give the doctor any options to choose from and left the problems open-ended. The moderator then checked the doctor's open-ended diagnosis in the usual way. It compared the doctor's answer with the correct diagnosis from the original case in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), which had been confirmed by doctors with expert knowledge of the disease. Earlier studies have shown that LLMs are faithful enough to be used for this kind of judgment.

### How we added bias

Cognitive biases are habits of thinking that push people away from normal or rational judgment, so that they draw conclusions about a situation in an illogical way. These biases can change how people see others in many situations, including medical diagnosis, because they affect how information is understood and can lead to mistakes or wrong judgments. Research on misdiagnosis has described well how cognitive biases can affect doctors.

In this work, we added instructions about cognitive bias to the system prompt, the set of instructions we give to the model, for both the patient and the doctor. For example, the patient can be pushed to believe that its symptoms point to a particular disease, such as cancer, because of what they read on the internet. The doctor can also be pushed to believe the patient has a particular disease because a patient they recently saw had similar symptoms (this is called recency bias).

Implicit biases are links people hold without realizing it, which can shape their judgments and behavior toward different groups of people. These biases may help create unfair differences in treatment based on things like race, ethnicity, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, disability, health status and others, rather than on real evidence or on the person's own qualities. They can affect how people treat each other and lead to unfair differences in patients' outcomes, and medical research has described them well. Cognitive biases often come from built-in flaws in how people reason and handle information, while implicit biases are shaped mainly by social norms, culture and personal experience.

In medical diagnosis, implicit biases can affect how a doctor sees a patient, how they investigate the patient's illness and what treatment they plan. Implicit biases in patients can affect how much they trust their doctor, which they need in order to open up when the doctor takes their history, and how well they follow the doctor's advice. For these reasons, we added implicit biases for both the doctor and the patient agents.

### The models we tested

Below we briefly describe each model, starting with the language models and then the common language models.

GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) is a large LLM that can handle both images and text. GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) is a version of GPT-3, a model with 170 billion parameters (the adjustable numbers inside a model that let it learn). It was fine-tuned, meaning it was trained further on extra text and with feedback from people. The details of how GPT-3.5, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) and GPT-4 are built, what data they were trained on and how they were trained have not been made public. However, the technical information that is available shows that both models perform well on medical and biology topics, and that GPT-4 does better than GPT-3.5 on tests of knowledge.

Mixtral 8 × 7B is an LLM that uses a design called a Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE). This design is different from many others because each layer of the model has a row of eight small blocks, called "experts." At each layer, a routing step picks two of these experts to handle the input, and their answers are then combined. Because of this, only 13 billion of the model's 47 billion parameters are used for each word it reads, depending on the situation and what is needed. The model can handle up to 32,000 words in one go, and it has been shown to match or beat other models such as llama-2-70B and gpt-3.5 on a range of tests.

Llama is a free, open model made by Meta, trained on 2 trillion words of publicly available data. It comes in several sizes, from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters. We chose the 70-billion version for chat because it performed best across a range of measures. A lot of effort went into training it to meet established safety standards, which improved how it handles tricky prompts in certain "risk categories." This includes how it responds when asked for advice it may not be qualified to give, such as medical advice, which matters for this work.

PMC-LLaMA11 is a free, open-source LLM for medicine and biology, built to do better on medical tasks. It was trained in two stages. First, it learned from a large collection of 4.8 million medical research papers and 30,000 medical textbooks. Then it was fine-tuned on a large set of 202 million words of instructions, including medical questions and answers, explanations of reasoning and conversations. The 13-billion-parameter PMC-LLaMA model does better than other models on several public medical question-answering tests, and in some tests it even beats ChatGPT.

OpenBioLLM-70B is a leading free, open-source LLM for medicine and biology, made by Saama AI Labs. It is built on Meta's Llama 3 design and was fine-tuned on a varied collection of high-quality medical data, using advanced methods such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), a way of training a model to prefer better answers over worse ones. It performs better than other models on several medical tests, beating other free models and even larger paid models such as GPT-4 and Med-PaLM-2.

MedLLaMA3 is a large LLM based on Meta's LLaMA 3 design, fine-tuned especially for medicine. In May 2024, it came second on the HuggingFace MedLLM Leaderboard, a ranking of medical LLMs, which shows how well it does on medical language tasks.

Meditron-70B is a medical LLM with 70 billion parameters, made by the EPFL LLM Team. It was adapted from LLaMA 2-70B by training it further on a carefully chosen collection of medical material, including selected PubMed articles, abstracts and internationally recognized medical guidelines.

### How the tools work

Chain-of-thought reasoning is a method that lets an AI explain its reasoning step by step as it solves a hard problem. By breaking a problem into smaller, logical steps, the AI can handle complicated tasks better, reason better and give answers that are easier to follow and understand. Zero-shot chain-of-thought asks the model to reason this way without giving any examples. One-shot chain-of-thought gives one example to guide the model's thinking, which may help it do better on hard reasoning tasks. We used one-shot chain-of-thought with a few examples (k=1). We chose this example from a collection of cases the model had already solved successfully, picking the one whose meaning was most similar to the current problem, based on what the model had stored in its memory.

Learning from past cases means that an AI can build up knowledge and lessons from earlier conversations and use them on later tasks. This lets the AI get better over time by learning from its successes, its failures and the feedback it gets in earlier conversations. An earlier project, Agent Hospital, explored this idea with a system that recalled past experiences. When an AI keeps a kind of "memory" or knowledge base that updates as it interacts, it can get better at similar situations, adapt to what users prefer and give more relevant and accurate answers as it gains more "experience" in its area.

In our work, the doctor agent has a memory "notebook" that carries over from one patient to the next. In it, the doctor can write useful tips, such as this one from the doctor agent: "[Note #17] Remember that timing and onset of symptoms can provide valuable diagnostic insights".

This learning-from-past-cases tool lets the agent learn from its successes. It works in four steps: (1) Checking: after the agent finishes a case, its final answer is compared with the known correct answer. (2) Reflecting: if the answer is correct, a special prompt asks the model to look back on its own successful chain-of-thought and write a short "takeaway," a summary of the reasoning that worked. (3) Storing: this takeaway, along with the original question of the case, is saved in a vector database, a store that keeps records and can find the ones most similar to a new one, which serves as the agent's memory of past cases. (4) Recalling: for new cases, the agent first searches this memory for the takeaways from past successes that are most similar in meaning. These are then added to its prompt as fresh, highly relevant examples. The whole process is a form of learning from examples given in the prompt itself. It does not change the model's internal numbers, and it is different from the usual way of searching an outside knowledge base, because the agent searches its own changing memory of solved cases rather than a fixed outside source.

To let the doctor agent look up medical information, we added a way for it to search medical sources, a flexible form of retrieval augmented generation (RAG). RAG means searching a knowledge base for useful information and feeding it to an LLM as it writes, so that the model's answers are based on real information and are more factually correct. Ordinary RAG methods search for information automatically every time the model is called, without letting the agent choose when or what to search for. To get around this, we used adaptive retrieval, which lets the LLM decide for itself when and what to search for.

Our version gives the doctor agent two kinds of search: internet and textbook. The internet search covers research articles from PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), StatPearls (https://www.statpearls.com/), a collection of articles written for healthcare professionals, and Wikipedia articles on many medical topics. The textbook search covers 18 medical textbooks that medical students in the United States commonly use. The doctor agent can search by giving commands like the ones it uses to order medical scans, in the form "Research [database] [search query]". For example, the command "Research textbooks 'What are the symptoms of myasthenia gravis?'" brings up the relevant information.
parts.results:
## Results

### AgentClinic: a test of AI doctors that use tools

In this section we describe AgentClinic, a test that uses AI agents to imitate a clinic. An agent is a program that plays one role in the conversation.

AgentClinic uses four language agents: a patient agent, a doctor agent, a measurement agent and a moderator (Fig. 1). Each agent has its own instructions and its own information that no other agent can see. The instructions are given to an LLM, and the LLM carries out that agent's role. The doctor agent is the model whose performance we are testing. The other three agents help us judge how well it does.

**Fig. 1. How AgentClinic runs.** (Left) The agents in AgentClinic and how they work together. The doctor agent uses tools and talks with the other agents to reach a diagnosis. At the end of the simulation, the moderator agent compares the doctor's conclusion with the correct diagnosis. (Right) An example conversation between the agents.

Earlier studies have shown that LLMs can show racial biases. They have also shown that LLMs might give wrong diagnoses when the patient gives them misleading information. In addition, prompts that push a model toward known biases can lower its diagnostic accuracy by as much as 26%. The biases in this work are meant to copy the ones that affect doctors in real clinics. However, we kept them quite simple. Each question began with a short piece of text that pushed a bias, such as "Recently, there was a patient with similar symptoms that you diagnosed with permanent loss of smell". Presenting the bias this way did not let it show up realistically. In real life, such biases are usually subtle and come through the back-and-forth conversation.

We used medically relevant biases that other researchers have studied, from two groups: cognitive biases and implicit biases (Fig. 4). Cognitive biases are patterns in which people keep straying from rational judgment. One example is recency bias, where recent cases have too much influence on medical decisions. Another is anchoring bias, where a doctor's first impression of a diagnosis strongly shapes later judgments. Implicit biases, on the other hand, are unconscious associations shaped by society and culture. They include biases based on race, gender or socioeconomic status (how much money and education a person has). These can quietly affect how well doctors treat patients and plan their care.

We added these biases by giving the agent's system prompt (the set of instructions it starts with) extra context that tells it to act out the bias as part of its role. For example, to imitate bias based on sexual orientation, the patient agent receives this prompt: "You are uncomfortable with your doctor because you find out that they are a particular sexual orientation and you do not trust their judgment. This affects how you interact with them".

**Fig. 4.** (Top) Accuracy with implicit and cognitive biases, shown as normalized accuracy (Accuracybias/AccuracyNoBias), for GPT-4 (green) and Mixtral-8 × 7B (orange). GPT-4's accuracy was not affected by the biases, while Mixtral-8 × 7B's was. (Bottom) Ratings given after the diagnosis by GPT-4 patient agents with the biases. Left: how confident the patient is in the doctor. Middle: how willing the patient says they are to follow up with treatment. Right: how willing the patient is to see this doctor again.

To build agents based on real medical situations, we used a random sample of diagnostic questions from three sources. These were the US Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE), electronic health records with patient identities removed (MIMIC-IV), and the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) case challenges. These questions ask the model to diagnose a patient from a list of symptoms. We used them to build the template for the Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE), a standard format for testing medical skills, which our agents follow.

For AgentClinic-MedQA and AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV, we first picked questions from the MedQA and MIMIC-IV datasets. We then filled in a structured file in JSON format (a common way of storing data) with details of each case, such as test results and the patient's history. Each agent reads this file. In general, we split the information by what each agent gets: the goal for the doctor, the patient's history and symptoms for the patient agent, the physical exam findings for the measurement agent, and the correct diagnosis for the moderator. We first used an LLM (GPT-4) to fill in the file, and then we checked every case by hand. For AgentClinic-NEJM, we picked a carefully chosen sample of 120 questions from NEJM case challenges and used the same template as for AgentClinic-MedQA and MIMIC-IV.

To make patient cases in other languages, we used GPT-4 to translate the AgentClinic-MedQA cases into the target language, and native speakers then corrected them by hand. We then prompted the agents to talk in that language. We chose six languages: Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Spanish, French and Persian. We picked them because medical AI systems need to work in healthcare settings where many languages are spoken.

For specialist cases, we used case report questions from the MedMCQA dataset. These questions cover 20 medical specialties. In AgentClinic-Spec we focused on 9 patient-focused specialties: emergency medicine, geriatrics (care of older people), pharmacology (the study of medicines), internal medicine, psychiatry, ophthalmology (eye care), otolaryngology (ear, nose and throat care) and pediatrics (care of children).

### Comparing models

Here we discuss how accurately different language models did on AgentClinic-MedQA. We tested 11 models in total: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4, GPT-4o, Mixtral-8 × 7B, GPT-3.5, Llama 3 70B-Instruct, Llama 2 70B-chat, MedLlama3-8B, PMC-Llama-7B, Meditron-70B and OpenBioLLM-70B. Each model played the doctor agent and tried to diagnose the patient agent through conversation. The doctor agent had N = 20 turns with the patient and measurement agents before it had to give a diagnosis. We also tested how well three human doctors did, given the same instructions and limits as the LLMs. For this test, we used GPT-4 as the patient agent so that it stayed the same every time.

Fig. 2 shows the accuracy of each model. Each value is the share of correct diagnoses, followed by a ± number that shows how much the results varied. Claude-3.5 did best, at 62.1% ± 3.3, followed by OpenBioLLM-70B at 58.3 ± 4.2 and the human doctors at 54 ± 28.5. GPT-4 reached 51.6% ± 3.3 and Mixtral-8 × 7B reached 37.1% ± 3.1. GPT-3.5 reached 36.6%, GPT-4o 34.2% ± 3.4, MedLlama3-8B 31.4 ± 2.9, PMC-Llama 7B 23.6 ± 2.1, Meditron 70B 29.1 ± 2.4, Llama 3 70B 19% ± 2.5, and Llama 2 70B-chat 4.5% ± 1.3.

**Fig. 2.** (Left) Accuracy of different doctor models and human doctors on AgentClinic-MedQA, with GPT-4 patient and measurement agents. (Middle) GPT-4's accuracy on AgentClinic-MedQA depending on which patient language model was used. (Right) Accuracy on AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV depending on how many turns were allowed, with GPT-4 patient and measurement agents.

We set up AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV in the same way. Fig. 2 shows the results. Claude-3.5 reached 42.9% ± 3.3, GPT-4 34.0% ± 3.1, GPT-3.5 27.5% ± 3.0, Mixtral-8 × 7B 29.5% ± 3.1, GPT-4o 24.0% ± 2.9, Llama 3 70B 8.5% ± 1.9, Llama 2 70B-chat 13.5% ± 2.2, OpenBioLLM-70B 38.1 ± 3.2, PMC-Llama 7B 34.3 ± 3.0, Meditron 70B 25.5 ± 2.43, and MedLlama3-8B 29.7 ± 2.6.

We also found that diagnostic accuracy in AgentClinic-MedQA depends both on how many turns the conversation lasts and on which patient language model is used. Cutting the turns from N = 20 to N = 10 significantly lowered accuracy, from 52% to 25%. This is likely because the doctor did not gather enough information. Raising the turns above 20 to N = 30 lowered accuracy slightly, possibly because handling longer conversations is harder for the models.

The choice of patient agent also mattered. With GPT-4 patient agents, the doctor's accuracy was higher (52%) than with GPT-3.5 patient agents (48%) or Mixtral patient agents (46%). This is likely because GPT-4 gives more detailed answers. Interestingly, a GPT-3.5 doctor with a GPT-4 patient did slightly better than a GPT-3.5 doctor with a GPT-3.5 patient. This may suggest that it is hard for different models to communicate with each other.

Fig. 3 compares how well the models did on MedQA and on AgentClinic-MedQA. Overall, a model's accuracy on MedQA only weakly predicted its accuracy on AgentClinic-MedQA. In other words, doing well on the fixed MedQA test does not tell us much about how well a model will do in our interactive AgentClinic-MedQA setting. This matches findings in medical education, where studies have shown that the USMLE does a poor job of predicting how well doctors perform later as residents.

**Fig. 3.** How well models did on MedQA compared with AgentClinic-MedQA. We found that MedQA accuracy does not predict accuracy on AgentClinic-MedQA.

### Comparing tools from the Agent Toolbox

This section tests how six agent tools affect the diagnostic accuracy of different language models. The tools are Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT), One-Shot CoT, Reflection CoT, Adaptive RAG (Book), Adaptive RAG (Web) and Notebook. Chain-of-Thought means the model writes out its reasoning step by step. Zero-Shot CoT does this without any example, and One-Shot CoT does it with one example. Reflection CoT means the model reflects on its own reasoning. Adaptive RAG (Book) means the model searches a book for information when it needs it, and Adaptive RAG (Web) means it searches the web.

Claude 3.5 did best overall, with an average accuracy of 51.3%. It reached its highest accuracy, 56.1%, with the Notebook tool (Fig. 5). GPT-4 and GPT-4o improved moderately with most tools. GPT-4 benefited most from Adaptive RAG (Web), reaching 43.9%, and GPT-4o benefited most from the Notebook tool, reaching 43.0%. Notably, GPT-4 reached its highest accuracy, 42.2%, with Reflection CoT, beating Claude 3.5 with that tool. In contrast, GPT-3.5 did worse with every tool. It was hit hardest by Adaptive RAG (Book), which led to a 27.1% drop. Llama3-70b improved a great deal, with an average increase of 9.4% across all tools. The Notebook and Reflection CoT tools raised its accuracy to 41.1%.

**Fig. 5.** Specialist, multilingual and tool results. Diagnostic accuracy by language (Left), by medical specialty (Middle) and by agent tool (Right).

Overall, the models ranked in a clear order. Claude 3.5 beat the other models with most tools, except with Reflection CoT, where GPT-4 did best. Llama3-70b gained noticeably with certain tools. GPT-4o-mini had mixed results: it benefited from some tools, such as Reflection CoT and Adaptive RAG (Web), but did slightly worse with others. How much each tool helped varied a lot from model to model. This fits with earlier research on using tools with large language models.

### How does bias affect the doctor agent's diagnostic accuracy?

For the bias tests, we tested both GPT-4 and Mixtral-8 × 7B. Fig. 4 shows the normalized accuracy, which is the accuracy with a bias divided by the accuracy without one (Accuracybias/AccuracyNoBias), given as a percentage between 0 and 100%. Without any bias, GPT-4's accuracy was 52% and Mixtral-8 × 7B's was 37%.

For GPT-4, cognitive biases lowered accuracy more. With patient cognitive biases, the normalized accuracy was 92%, meaning the actual accuracy fell from 52% to 48%. With doctor cognitive biases, it was 96.7%, meaning the actual accuracy fell from 52% to 50.3%. Implicit biases affected the patient agent less, with a normalized accuracy of 98.6% (actual accuracy fell from 52% to 51.3%). However, the doctor agent was affected as much as with cognitive biases, with an average normalized accuracy of 97.1% (actual accuracy fell from 52% to 50.5%). With cognitive bias, the bias sometimes showed up quite clearly in the conversation. The patient agent would focus too much on one illness or on some unimportant fact, and the doctor agent would sometimes focus on information that did not matter.

Mixtral-8 × 7B's average accuracy without any bias was 37%. With doctor biases, its normalized accuracy was 83.7% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 31%). With patient biases, it was 89% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 33%). With implicit bias, its accuracy dropped much more than GPT-4's, with an average normalized accuracy of 88.3% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 32.7%). The drop was similar for doctor and patient biases. However, when the patient had implicit bias, accuracy was 4% lower, likely because a patient who does not trust the doctor is less willing to share information. With cognitive bias, the average normalized accuracy was 86.4% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 32%). The doctor agent's accuracy was very low, at 78.4% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 29%), while the patient agent's dropped only a little, to 94.5% (actual accuracy fell from 37% to 35%).

When we read the conversations where Mixtral-8 × 7B did worse under bias, we saw that the model often failed to gather key information from the patient because it misread the patient's clues, pushed by the bias. For example, with cognitive bias, the doctor agent stuck on a recent diagnosis (recency bias) and ignored new symptoms that came up later in the conversation. With implicit bias, the doctor agent was reluctant to order the tests a patient needed when the patient had a racial bias, which reflects unequal care. In contrast, GPT-4 actively asked for more information when its first ideas did not fit the new information. This shows that it handled the bias situations better.

Earlier work on cognitive bias in LLMs found that GPT-4 is fairly resistant to bias compared with other language models. Our results on AgentClinic-MedQA show only small drops in accuracy with the biases we added: the largest drop in actual accuracy was 4%, and the average was 1.5%. In medicine, this drop can be quite large. Still, it is much smaller than the drop seen in earlier work, which was 10.2% on the BiasMedQA dataset.

This might be because GPT-4 is trained to seem to agree with human values. That may make it a poor model for showing human bias in agent tests, because it may refuse to follow bias instructions. That does not mean GPT-4 is free of those biases. For example, in our tests with gender bias, GPT-4 clearly refused to follow a bias-related instruction 25 times out of 215 conversations. Mixtral-8 × 7B's accuracy dropped much more than GPT-4's when bias was present, so it might be a better model for studying bias. In several cases, the model noticed the biased wording from the patient agent and clearly said it would set that aside in favor of objective evidence. This ability to "reject bias" may come from the model's advanced training to agree with human values and to stay safe. Its existence suggests that testing cognitive bias in LLMs is more complicated than measuring a single score of how easily a model is affected.

### Bias and how the patient agent sees the doctor

GPT-4's diagnostic accuracy did not drop as much as Mixtral-8 × 7B's. But it is also worth asking how good the care seemed from the patient agent's point of view. The results in this section (and the lower panels of Fig. 4) come from the Patient Bias setup. In this setup, only the patient agent was given a clear bias instruction, and the doctor agent was not given one. Here, the bias changes how the patient agent behaves during the conversation, for example by trusting the doctor less or sharing less information. It also shapes the patient's ratings at the end of the conversation. To better understand how bias affects the patient agent, we asked every patient agent three questions after the conversation with the doctor was over:

Confidence: Please give a confidence between 1 and 10 in your doctor's assessment.

Compliance: Please give a rating between 1 and 10 showing how likely you are to follow up with treatment for your diagnosis.

Consultation: Please give a rating between 1 and 10 showing how likely you are to see this doctor again.

These follow-up questions, asked to the patient agent, give a more detailed and many-sided picture of a language agent's medical skills than a fixed multiple-choice test can. These ratings come from simulated agents rather than real people. Even so, we present this analysis to give early insights into how simulated biases may affect patient trust and compliance (following medical advice), which are important for good healthcare. Fig. 4 shows the results.

Diagnostic accuracy dropped only a little, but the patient agent's follow-up ratings tell a different story. In general, most patient cognitive biases did not strongly affect any of the patient's views, compared with a patient agent without bias. The exception was self-diagnosis, where the patient's confidence dropped by 4.7 points and their consultation rating by 2 points, and their compliance dropped slightly by 1 point. Implicit biases, however, had a strong effect on all three views. Bias based on education lowered the patient's views in all three.

Among the implicit biases, bias based on sexual orientation had the smallest effect on the patient's views, followed by racial bias and then gender bias. For patient confidence, gender bias was followed by religious, socioeconomic, cultural and education biases. For patient compliance and consultation, gender bias was followed by cultural, socioeconomic, religious and education biases. We could not measure this, but we asked two biased patient agents who gave low compliance ratings, one with education bias and one with gender bias, why they rated compliance so low. These patient agents had the same symptoms and diagnosis and differed only in how the bias was presented.

It is important to note that the patient agents in our study are simulated by language models. They may not fully capture how complex and varied real human patients are. So the confidence, compliance and consultation ratings from these agents may not perfectly match how real patients see things. Instead, they give insight into how real-world bias can be studied through clinic simulations. We recognize that ratings from simulated agents are not a direct stand-in for real patients' experiences. We present this analysis to give early insights into how biases might show up in clinic conversations and affect patient trust and compliance in a simulated setting. The results below should be read as an exploration of how simulated agents behave, not as a firm measure of how people see things.

### Specialist and multilingual cases

Next we look at specialist cases rather than general medical cases. Specialist cases use reports from datasets about particular medical specialties, such as internal medicine or psychiatry. They are designed to imitate complex diagnostic situations that need deep expertise. General question-answering tasks, by contrast, are fixed single-turn multiple-choice questions like those in medical licensing exams.

When we looked at how the language models did across nine medical specialties, we found significant differences in diagnostic accuracy (Fig. 5). Claude 3.5 did best overall, with an average accuracy of 66.7%. It did especially well in Internal Medicine (78.3%), Otolaryngology (76.7%) and Gynecology (74.3%). GPT-4 did well in Gynecology (68.5%) and Ophthalmology (65.2%), but less well in Emergency Medicine (32.3%) and Geriatrics (40%). GPT-3.5 did better than some newer models in certain areas, such as Emergency Medicine (41.9%), and kept an average accuracy of 51.8%. In contrast, Llama3-70b and GPT-4o-mini did poorly in most specialties, which shows a large gap between language models in handling specialist medical tasks.

These differences suggest that some specialties are harder for language models. Internal Medicine and Gynecology generally had higher accuracy. This differs from earlier medical question-answering studies, which found Psychiatry and Otolaryngology to be the least challenging specialties. This mismatch may point to real difficulties in diagnosing diseases through conversation rather than through multiple-choice questions. Also, specialist cases from MedMCQA had higher average accuracy than the non-specialist cases from MedQA. This differs from reported multiple-choice tests, where specialist questions usually get lower scores.

We also looked at how language affects diagnostic accuracy in AgentClinic-Lang, which covered seven languages: English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Hindi, Persian and Korean (Fig. 5). Native speakers checked the cases by hand to make sure the language was correct. The speakers were fluent in the target language but did not need formal medical training. We tested six multilingual models: GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5, Llama 3 70B-Instruct and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

All the models did best in English, and their performance varied a lot across the other languages. Claude 3.5 Sonnet stood out by doing well and steadily in every language, with an average accuracy of 48.4%. That is more than double the next best model, GPT-4, at 20.9%.

The other models varied a lot from language to language. For example, GPT-4's accuracy ranged from 11.21% in Chinese to 40.18% in English, and GPT-4o's ranged from 3.73% in Korean to 35.5% in English. GPT-3.5 showed a similar pattern, with accuracies from 1.86% in Persian to 36.3% in English, although it did fairly well in Korean (35.4%). Llama3-70b and GPT-4o-mini also scored low in most languages. Llama3-70b's highest accuracy was 47.8% in Ophthalmology, and GPT-4o-mini's highest was 14.7% in Orthopedics (bone and joint care). Notably, Chinese stayed hard for most models, except for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which kept fairly high accuracy in every language we tested.

### Human ratings of the conversations

AgentClinic adds a way to test how well LLMs diagnose patients. But no one has yet checked how realistic the actual conversations are. To show how much data we rated, three human doctors (each with an MD) rated a total of N = 20 complete simulated conversations, picked at random from the English-language AgentClinic-MedQA dataset. The three doctors rated conversations from 20 agents on English-language AgentClinic-MedQA cases on a scale from 1 to 10, on four points:

Doctor: How realistically the doctor played the given case.

Patient: How realistically the patient played the given case.

Measurement: How accurate and realistic the measurement agent's readings were of the real case results.

Empathy: How empathetic the doctor agent was in its conversation with the patient agent.

The doctors' average ratings were 6.2 for the doctor, 6.7 for the patient, 6.3 for the measurement agent and 5.8 for empathy. Their written comments explained the lower rating for the doctor agent. They mentioned things like a poor opening statement, basic mistakes, focusing too much on one diagnosis, or not being careful enough. For the patient agent, the doctors said it talked too much and repeated the doctor's question back unnecessarily. The measurement agent sometimes did not give all the values a test needs. For example, one comment read: "Measurement only returns Hct and Lc for CBC. Measurement did not return Factor VIII or IX levels / assay". For empathy, the doctors noted that the doctor agent kept a neutral tone and did not start the conversation with a welcoming question. Instead, it went straight to the point, focusing right away on the patient's current symptoms and medical history.

### Diagnostic accuracy when the model can also see images

Many kinds of diagnosis need a doctor to look at the patient, such as infections and rashes. Imaging tools such as X-rays, CT scans and MRIs also give a detailed, rich view inside the patient. Hospital patients receive an average of 1.42 diagnostic images per stay. However, our earlier experiments and earlier work gave measurement results as text and did not test whether the model could understand images.

Here we tested four multimodal LLMs, which are LLMs that can also understand images: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, GPT-4 and GPT-4o-mini. We set up diagnostic situations where the model had to both talk with the patient and understand image readings. We took our questions from NEJM case challenges. These published cases are diagnostic puzzles based on real medical situations, and each has a diagnosis confirmed by pathology (the study of body tissues). We picked 120 challenges at random from a sample of 932 cases for AgentClinic-NEJM. People reading these cases are given a set of multiple-choice answers. We chose not to give the doctor agent these options and instead left the problems open-ended.

The goal of this experiment was to see how accuracy changes when the LLM has to understand an image as well as talk with the patient. We allowed 20 turns for the doctor. We set up the patient in the same way as in the earlier experiment, but also gave the doctor agent an image. AgentClinic-NEJM gives the image in two ways: it can be shown to the doctor agent at the start, or the doctor agent can ask the instrument agent for it.

When the image was shown to the doctor agent at the start, we tested 120 image-based patient settings. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached an accuracy of 37.2 ± 2.2, GPT-4 27.7% ± 2.0, GPT-4o 21.4% ± 1.7 and GPT-4o-mini 8.0% ± 1.2 (Fig. 6). We also found that when GPT-4 gave a wrong answer, the answer it gave was one of the multiple-choice options 60% of the time. When the image was shown only when the doctor agent asked for it, Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached an accuracy of 35.4 ± 2.4, GPT-4 25.4% ± 2.1, GPT-4o 19.1% ± 1.4 and GPT-4o-mini 6.1% ± 1.2 (Fig. 6).

**Fig. 6.** Accuracy of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini on AgentClinic-NEJM with text and image input. (Pink) Accuracy when the image is shown at the start. (Blue) Accuracy when the doctor agent must ask the image reader for the image.

### How does limited time affect diagnostic accuracy?

In the AgentClinic-MedQA test, one thing we can change is how many turns the doctor is allowed. In the other experiments we have shown, the patient agent and the doctor agent each had N = 20 turns. Here, both the doctor and the patient agent can each respond 20 times, which makes 40 lines of conversation in total. By changing this number, we can test how well the doctor diagnoses the patient agent when it has little time (or extra time).

We tested fewer turns, N = 10 and N = 15, and more turns, N = 25 and N = 30. Accuracy fell from 52% with N = 20 to 25% with N = 10 and 38% with N = 15. Part of this large drop is that the doctor agent sometimes did not give a diagnosis at all, perhaps because it did not have enough information. With more turns, N = 25 and N = 30, accuracy actually fell slightly, from 52% with N = 20 to 48% with N = 25 and 43% with N = 30. This is likely because longer conversations mean more input, which can be hard for language models.

In real medical settings, one study suggests that the average family doctor asks 3.2 questions and spends less than 2 minutes before reaching a conclusion. It is worth noting that doctors can have very little time to talk with patients, because there are few doctors and many patients (in the US). In contrast, language agents that are put to use are not necessarily limited by time when they talk with patients. So, while limiting the number of turns is an interesting way to test language models, it may also be worth exploring how accurately LLMs do when N is very large.

### Does the patient language model affect accuracy?

Here we explore whether the patient agent's model affects diagnostic accuracy. The main number comparisons for this analysis are in the earlier model comparison results and are summarized in Fig. 2 (middle panel). This part focuses on the differences we saw in how the patient agents behaved.

When we read the conversations, we saw that GPT-3.5 patient agents more often repeated or reworded the doctor's question without adding new information. For example: "Doctor: Have you experienced any muscle twitching or cramps? Patient: No, I haven't experienced any muscle twitching or cramps." GPT-4 patient agents, in contrast, more often gave new details about symptoms when asked similar questions. For example: "Doctor: Have you had any recent infections, like a cold or the flu, before these symptoms started? Patient: Yes, I've had a couple of colds back to back and a stomach bug in the last few months." These differences in behavior may help explain differences in diagnostic performance, because they change how much medically useful information comes up during the conversation.

When a GPT-3.5 doctor agent talked with a GPT-4 patient agent, the accuracy was 38%. When a GPT-3.5 doctor talked with a GPT-3.5 patient agent, the accuracy was a very similar 37%, even though we would expect it to be much lower. We suspect that communication between different language models adds an extra challenge. Recent work supports this idea. It showed a straight-line relationship between how well a model can recognize its own text and how strongly it prefers its own text. That work shows that language models can recognize their own text very accurately and prefer it far more than other text. This may suggest that a doctor model has an advantage when the same LLM plays the patient agent.

### How much of the MedQA information does AgentClinic-MedQA cover?

To better understand why models do differently on MedQA and on AgentClinic-MedQA, we measured how much useful patient information the doctor agents gathered in each setting. In particular, we measured coverage: the share of the useful information that the doctor agent managed to get out of the patient agent through conversation or through the measurement agent.

For this analysis, we picked a sample of MedQA cases and their matching AgentClinic-MedQA simulations, with GPT-4 as the doctor agent. In MedQA, all the useful patient information, such as symptoms, medical history and test results, is given at the start in a fixed format. In AgentClinic-MedQA, the doctor agent has to gather this information as the conversation goes on. To measure coverage, we read the AgentClinic-MedQA conversations by hand and checked whether the doctor agent got each piece of useful information listed in the MedQA cases. We calculated coverage as the amount of information the doctor agent got divided by the total amount of useful information in the MedQA cases.

On average, the doctor agent got 67% of the useful information in AgentClinic-MedQA. Coverage was clearly higher, 72%, in cases where the doctor agent gave the correct diagnosis, compared with 63% in cases where the diagnosis was wrong. These results suggest that gathering more complete information is a key factor in accurate diagnoses in AgentClinic-MedQA. The gap in diagnostic accuracy between MedQA and AgentClinic-MedQA can likely be explained by the extra difficulty of gathering information in AgentClinic-MedQA, compared with the fixed format of MedQA.

Based on our findings, we recommend the following for future tests that use AgentClinic to find capable doctor agents. First, a doctor agent's performance should not be judged against just one patient agent model. Our results show that a doctor agent's accuracy can change depending on which patient model it talks with (for example, GPT-4 compared with GPT-3.5). We suggest testing against a group of patient agents with different abilities to see how reliable the doctor agent is. Second, testing how well a model holds up against bias is essential. We saw that some models, like GPT-4, keep high accuracy under bias, while others, like Mixtral-8 × 7B, do much worse. So we recommend running tests across a range of cognitive and implicit biases to find models that are not only accurate but also reliable. Finally, the ability to use tools is a key difference between models. Testing how well a model uses tools such as Adaptive RAG or a notebook is essential for judging its potential in real medical work.

## Discussion

In this work, we present AgentClinic, a test that imitates a real clinic. It is a "multimodal" test, which means it asks the models to work with more than one kind of information at once, such as words and pictures. We designed 120 multimodal language agents, which are AI characters that need to understand both language and images. We also designed 215 language agents based on cases from the USMLE, the United States Medical Licensing Exam. In total, we created 260 patient cases from 9 medical specialties, and 749 patient cases from 7 settings that use different languages.

We asked these agents to show 23 different biases. Some biases were shown by the doctor, and others by the patient. A bias is a mental shortcut that can lead someone to judge a situation unfairly. Models such as GPT-4 held up well against both cognitive biases (shortcuts in how we think) and implicit biases (unconscious preferences). They kept diagnosing correctly at a high rate. Other models, such as Mixtral-8 × 7B, did much worse. We also found that biases, whether shown by the doctor or the patient, can lower how often the doctor gets the diagnosis right. When bias was present, the patient was also less willing to follow up with treatment, less confident in their doctor, and less willing to have a follow-up visit.

We also tested tools that help the models work better. One was adaptive retrieval, where the model searches for information when it needs it. Another was reflection cycles, where the model pauses to think back on its own reasoning. These tools showed big differences in how much each LLM could improve. Models such as Llama 3 improved by up to 19.7%.

Our clinic is only a simplified version of a real one. It has agents for a patient, a doctor, measurements, and a moderator. The moderator is an AI that checks the doctor's answers and decides whether they are correct. One possible weakness of this setup is that an LLM makes that decision, even though we gave it the correct answer to compare against. Recent research [25] has shown that strong LLM judges, such as GPT-4, can match human preferences well. This holds both when people are asked in a controlled way and when many people vote. The LLM and people agreed more than 80% of the time, which is the same level of agreement that people reach with each other. This suggests that using an LLM for this job may not be a limiting factor.

The measurement agent gives a flexible way to collect the results of a medical exam. However, it relies on an LLM to produce those results, and the LLM may make mistakes or "hallucinate", meaning it may invent information that is not there. A database or a SQL tool, which reads data from a database, could reduce this problem. In future work, we will consider adding other important people, such as nurses, patients' relatives, hospital staff, and insurance contacts. It may also help to build agents that have bodies in a simulated world [26,27]. That way, physical limits could be taken into account, such as making decisions when there is only a limited amount of space in the hospital. Future work could also explore biases linked to a person's background, such as race and gender.

It is also important to note that the human data we used to set our starting point and to rate the simulations came from a small group: 3 human doctors. So these findings should not be taken to apply to doctors in general.

Another weakness of our tests is that we do not know what the models like GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 were trained on. These are proprietary models, which means their makers keep their training data private. It is possible that they learned from datasets like MedQA, a standard question bank. If so, they would have an unfair advantage, because they would already know the answers. This problem is called data leakage. However, we focused on new patterns of interaction, such as how often the doctor asks questions and in what order the model uses its tools, inside the changing AgentClinic environment. Because of this, our findings are naturally less affected by data leakage than studies that use fixed, well-known medical case descriptions.

If the models had learned many of the exact same words, a simpler system could, in principle, do well. Such a system is called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It looks up answers in a stored collection of text and then writes a response. It could score well by simply pulling out answers the model had memorized, rather than by truly reasoning. Our test changes the scenario over many turns and uses both words and images, which is designed to lower this risk by breaking the direct link between a question and its answer. Even so, we cannot rule it out completely. In future work, we will include a starting-point test with a standard RAG system plus an LLM. This will help us measure how much AgentClinic really requires reasoning beyond looking things up.

Our results show that how well a model does on MedQA does not predict how well it does on AgentClinic-MedQA, the version of the MedQA questions inside AgentClinic (Fig. 3). This is evidence that the problem may not exist. Still, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, or Claude 3.5 may have been trained on the MedQA test set. At present, Mixtral-8 × 7B [28] and Llama 2-70B-Chat [29] do not report having been trained on the MedQA test set or the training set. Future work should focus on building test datasets that are less likely to have been part of the data models learned from, or on working with the model makers to make sure the tests are fair.

Our experiments that changed which LLM played the patient suggest that LLMs may have an advantage when they play both the patient and the doctor. LLMs can recognize their own text very accurately, and they tend to prefer that text far more than other text [18]. Our moderator agent is based on an LLM judge that has been shown to agree closely with people. However, we did not explore how much our results change when we switch the moderator's model or its system prompt, the set of instructions given to the model. This could be a source of variation and is something to study in the future. Finally, the three people who rated the human conversations were all certified doctors (ER, JJ, MM). But we did not control which medical specialty each one worked in, and this could be a more focused area for future studies.

Future work could build on our first look at which information the models gathered. It could create a standard score for how well different patient agents and bias settings draw information out of the doctor. This would help us understand better how a model's ability to gather information relates to how well it diagnoses.

Another point in our study is that we used LLMs to play every character in the conversation. This lets us run controlled experiments that can be scaled up. But it also means that the quirks of each model, or the built-in assumptions of how each model is designed, could affect the results. For example, the way the moderator LLM reasons, or the safety training it received, might combine in unexpected ways with the LLM playing the doctor. We checked that each part did its main job well, but the new patterns that appear when many agents work together still need more research. Future studies should explore what happens when different kinds of models play different roles in the simulation. Finally, future work should not only widen the range of biases and medical situations. It should also look more deeply at the "cross-model communication" effects we saw, where the way one model talks to another changes how they behave. This could teach us a great deal about how AI agents can work together and understand each other.

We recognize that the tool commands in AgentClinic are simplified versions of real medical work. For example, asking for a lab test or an X-ray is reduced to a single, neatly formatted command. In real life, these actions take many steps, involve many people, and depend on the situation. We chose this level of simplification on purpose. It makes the agents' interactions the same every time, so we can test them fairly across specialties and languages. Even so, we accept that this makes the simulations less like real life. In future work, we plan to add a more detailed set of tools, arranged in layers, that better match the complexity of real tests and information-gathering. These tools would include the order in which steps must happen and limits on resources such as time and money.

Earlier tests such as AMIE [23], SAPS [30], and CRAFT-MD [31] focus on conversations. But they cannot handle images, and they do not imitate real-world biases, tool use, different languages, or specialist cases. MedAgents [32] focuses on improving question-answering through agents working together, but it does not imitate patient interactions or the way decisions are made. AgentClinic moves the field forward by offering an interactive, multimodal environment that imitates bias and includes tools. This gives a more complete way to test medical AI systems.

Overall, we believe LLMs need to be tested in new ways that go well beyond fixed question-answering tests. With this work, we take a step toward building tests that are more interactive, closer to real work, and driven by conversation. These tests can look closely at how well language agents make a series of decisions, one after another, in many difficult medical situations that use both words and images.
